opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest bottleneck isn't the modeling itself anymore. It's everything around it. When you look at how predictive modeling gets done in most enterprises today, the data lives in a relational database: customers, transactions, products, all spread across many tables connected by keys. To build a model, a data scientist has to flatten all of that into a single table. That means joins, aggregations, and a lot of manual feature engineering. That process can take months, and it's where most of the human effort and most of the errors go.

So the bottleneck is really the distance between the question the business wants to ask, something like "which customers are going to churn in the next 30 days?" or "what will this user buy next?", and having a working model in production that answers it. Each new question traditionally means a new pipeline, new features, and a new model. That doesn't scale. A company might have hundreds of prediction problems worth solving, but they only have the bandwidth to tackle a handful.

What we've been working on is learning directly on the relational data. You treat the database as a graph, where rows are nodes and primary-foreign key relationships are edges, and let graph neural networks, and now foundation models pretrained on relational data, learn the patterns themselves. That collapses the feature engineering step. You can go from a question to a prediction much faster, sometimes without training a task-specific model at all.

Once that technical barrier comes down, the remaining bottleneck becomes organizational. Do people know which questions to ask? Can they trust the predictions? Are the predictions actually wired into a decision process? A model that's 5% more accurate creates no value if nobody acts on its output. So I'd say the frontier is shifting from "can we build the model" to "can we integrate predictions into how the business actually operates," and that's a very exciting shift to be part of.

r001.rationale: The response says predictions must be wired into business decisions and that a more accurate model creates no value if nobody acts on its output, identifying integration into business operations as the remaining bottleneck to realizing value.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think the bottleneck is the modeling anymore. When we started Kumo, the hypothesis was that the hard part would be the algorithms, the graph neural networks, getting the architecture right. And that part is hard, but it's the part we actually know how to do. The real bottleneck is everything around the model.

Think about how predictive machine learning works in a typical enterprise today. You have a data warehouse, Snowflake or Databricks or BigQuery, with maybe hundreds of tables. And a data scientist who wants to predict, say, which customers are going to churn, has to spend weeks, sometimes months, flattening that relational data into a single feature table. Joining tables, aggregating transactions over the last thirty days, the last ninety days, hand-crafting features. Then they train an XGBoost model on top of that. Then they have to productionize it, keep the feature pipelines running, retrain when things drift. By the time you're done, you've built a bespoke system for one prediction task, and if the business asks a slightly different question next quarter, you start over.

So the bottleneck is that we've been treating every prediction problem as a one-off engineering project. And that means most companies can only afford to do a handful of them, usually the ones with an obvious nine-figure payoff. All the medium-sized opportunities, the ones where a model would be valuable but not worth a six-month data science project, never get built.

What we're trying to do is collapse that. If you treat the data warehouse itself as a graph, where tables are node types and foreign keys are edges, then a graph neural network can learn directly over the relational structure. The feature engineering becomes something the model learns rather than something a human writes. Then the question of what you want to predict becomes almost declarative. You write something that looks like a query: predict the sum of purchases for each customer over the next thirty days. And the system figures out the training data, the labels, the architecture.

And the second piece is the foundation model angle. We've seen in language and vision what happens when you pretrain on huge amounts of data and the model becomes general. Relational data has been the one modality where that hasn't happened yet, because every company's schema is different. But it turns out you can pretrain across many databases and get a model that transfers, that works zero-shot on a schema it's never seen. That's what changes the economics. If getting a prediction goes from months to minutes, the business can ask a hundred questions instead of three.

So, to answer directly: the bottleneck is the human labor between the data and the model. The modeling has become the easy part, and the goal is to make the rest disappear.

r001.rationale: The candidate identifies data preparation, feature engineering, and productionizing models as the bottleneck. It does not identify integrating predictions into downstream business decisions.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is getting from a business question to a prediction problem that you can actually act on. People often focus on the model, but before you get there, you have to understand what decision you’re trying to improve, what data is available at the time of that decision, and what outcome you want to predict.

And in a business, that data is usually spread across many different tables. You have customers, transactions, products, and relationships between them. Turning all of that into the right input for a model takes a lot of manual work and domain expertise.

So the opportunity is to make that process much easier. But you still have to close the loop: if I give you a better prediction, what do you do differently? A prediction creates business value when it changes a decision and that decision leads to a better outcome.

r001.rationale: The response names translating a business question into an actionable prediction, including preparing data, as the biggest bottleneck. It says predictions create value when they change decisions, but does not identify integrating predictions into downstream decision-making as the biggest bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest bottleneck is really connecting a prediction to a business action. You can build a model that predicts something very accurately, but then the question is, what do you do differently because of that prediction? Who acts on it, and how does that fit into their workflow?

That also means you have to start with the right problem. What decision are we trying to improve? What data is available at the time that decision is made? And how will we measure whether the model actually helped? The modeling is one piece, but getting that whole loop—from data to prediction to action to an outcome—to work is where a lot of the effort goes.

r001.rationale: The response identifies connecting predictions to business actions and fitting them into decision-makers’ workflows as the biggest bottleneck.
